steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the description section of an encyclopedia article on application firewalls: what application layer filtering is, and the difference between network-based and host-based application firewalls.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Application layer filtering in general
- Network-based application firewalls
- Host-based application firewalls

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Application layer filtering
  - higher level than traditional security appliances
  - decisions on more than source/destination IP address or ports; info across multiple connections per host
- Network-based
  - application layer of TCP/IP stack; understand protocols like FTP, DNS, HTTP
  - can spot unwanted apps/services on non standard port, or abuse of an allowed protocol
  - modern versions may include: encryption offloading, intrusion prevention system, data loss prevention
  - WAF = specialized network-based appliance, reverse proxy, inspects traffic before forwarding to server
- Host-based
  - monitors application system calls / general system communication
  - more granularity and control, but only protects its own host
  - filtering per process; prompts define rules for processes without a connection yet
  - further filtering by process ID of packet owner
  - often combined with / used alongside a packet filter
  - technological limitations -> sandboxing used as replacement to protect system processes

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Application layer filtering works at a higher level than traditional security appliances do. Because of this, packet decisions can be made based on more than just the source/destination IP Address or ports, and information that spans multiple connections for a given host can also be used.

### Network-based application firewalls

Network-based application firewalls work at the application layer of a TCP/IP stack and they can understand certain applications and protocols, such as File Transfer Protocol (FTP), Domain Name System (DNS), or Hypertext Transfer Protocol (HTTP). This lets it identify unwanted applications or services that use a non standard port, or detect if a protocol that is allowed is being abused.

Modern versions of network-based application firewalls can include these technologies:

Encryption offloading

Intrusion prevention system

Data loss prevention

Web application firewalls (WAF) are a specialized version of a network-based appliance. They act as a reverse proxy and inspect traffic before it is forwarded to the server they are associated with.

- Host-based
  - monitors application system calls / general system communication
  - more granularity and control, but only protects its own host
  - filtering per process; prompts define rules for processes without a connection yet
  - further filtering by process ID of packet owner
  - often combined with / used alongside a packet filter
  - technological limitations -> sandboxing used as replacement to protect system processes

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Application layer filtering works at a higher level than traditional security appliances do. Because of this, packet decisions can be made based on more than just the source/destination IP Address or ports, and information that spans multiple connections for a given host can also be used.

### Network-based application firewalls

Network-based application firewalls work at the application layer of a TCP/IP stack and they can understand certain applications and protocols, such as File Transfer Protocol (FTP), Domain Name System (DNS), or Hypertext Transfer Protocol (HTTP). This lets it identify unwanted applications or services that use a non standard port, or detect if a protocol that is allowed is being abused.

Modern versions of network-based application firewalls can include these technologies:

Encryption offloading

Intrusion prevention system

Data loss prevention

Web application firewalls (WAF) are a specialized version of a network-based appliance. They act as a reverse proxy and inspect traffic before it is forwarded to the server they are associated with.

### Host-based application firewalls

A host-based application firewall monitors application system calls or other general system communication. This gives more granularity and more control, but it can only protect the host that it is running on. Control is applied by filtering per process. Usually prompts are used to define rules for processes that have not received a connection yet. More filtering can be done by looking at the process ID of the owner of the data packets. Many host-based application firewalls are combined with a packet filter or used together with one.

Because of technological limitations, modern solutions like sandboxing are being used to replace host-based application firewalls for protecting system processes.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Application layer filtering operates at a higher level than traditional security appliances. This allows packet decisions to be made based on more than just source/destination IP Address or ports, and can also use information spanning multiple connections for any given host.

### Network-based application firewalls

Network-based application firewalls operate at the application layer of a TCP/IP stack[1] and can understand certain applications and protocols such as File Transfer Protocol (FTP), Domain Name System (DNS), or Hypertext Transfer Protocol (HTTP). This allows it to identify unwanted applications or services using a non standard port, or to detect if an allowed protocol is being abused.[2]

Modern versions of network-based application firewalls can include the following technologies:

Encryption offloading

Intrusion prevention system

Data loss prevention

Web application firewalls (WAF) are a specialized version of a network-based appliance that acts as a reverse proxy, inspecting traffic before it is forwarded to an associated server.

### Host-based application firewalls

A host-based application firewall monitors application system calls or other general system communication. This gives more granularity and control, but is limited to protecting only the host it is running on. Control is applied by filtering on a per process basis. Generally, prompts are used to define rules for processes that have not yet received a connection. Further filtering can be done by examining the process ID of the owner of the data packets. Many host-based application firewalls are combined with, or used in conjunction with, a packet filter.[3]

Due to technological limitations, modern solutions such as sandboxing are being used as a replacement for host-based application firewalls to protect system processes.[4]
